claims.text: A controlled increase of approximately 1 at.% phosphorus will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability relative to the baseline.
Increasing phosphorus will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to the baseline.
Additional phosphorus enhances chemical short-range order through stronger localized metallic–phosphorus bonding.
Stronger localized metallic–phosphorus bonding increases bonding constraints in the liquid.
Increased phosphorus promotes a more tightly interconnected amorphous structure with greater local bonding heterogeneity.
The phosphorus-induced structural changes reduce atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses crystalline nucleation and growth during cooling and mild thermal exposure.
The modified alloy will have a greater critical casting thickness or a lower critical cooling rate for amorphous solidification than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The beneficial effect should occur under rapid solidification and moderate annealing temperatures.
The beneficial effect is limited to an optimal phosphorus-composition window.
Excess phosphorus may cause phase separation or embrittlement.
At sufficiently high annealing temperatures, the thermodynamic drive for crystallization may override phosphorus-induced kinetic stabilization.
